sections.html:
Worcester is the main city of Central Massachusetts, about 40 miles west of Boston, and the seat of Worcester County. It had an estimated 213,862 residents in 2025, second in the state. Many of its houses are 19th-century triple-deckers, so rent and condition affect value. The city's Assessing Division values every parcel for tax.

DetailWorcester Assessing
OfficeCity Hall Room 209, 455 Main Street, Worcester, MA 01608
Phone and email508-799-1098, assessing@worcesterma.gov
HoursMonday to Friday, 8:30 a.m. to 5 p.m.
Fiscal yearJuly 1 to June 30
Valuation dateJanuary 1 before the fiscal year
Property classesResidential, Open Space, Commercial, Industrial

Bills go out four times a year, on July 1, October 1, January 1 and April 1, and each payment falls due 30 days after it is issued.

  • The July 1 and October 1 bills are preliminary, each equal to last year's tax divided by four.
  • The January 1 and April 1 bills are actual. They use the new assessment and rate, subtract the preliminary tax already billed, and split the rest between the two payments.
  • A change in your tax from reassessment therefore shows up only in the third and fourth quarters.

Posted rates are $13.28 per $1,000 of assessed value for residential property and $29.06 per $1,000 for commercial. No fiscal year is attached to them, so check the year printed on your bill before relying on either figure.

Massachusetts requires every city to assess property at full and fair cash value, and the Department of Revenue certifies Worcester's assessments after checking market sales and running valuation audits.

The city's process has three steps. The Assessor values all taxable property, classifies each parcel by use, and then applies the value and class to set the tax. January 1 is the tax date, so what you own and its condition that day drive the next fiscal year's bill.

Proposition 2 1/2 caps the city's total levy, not each owner's bill. The levy can rise 2.5 percent over the prior year plus tax from new construction. One house can climb faster than that if its value rose faster than other homes, and the city's position is that taxes are fair as long as the assessed value is accurate.

An abatement application is how you dispute a value or correct a billing error that made your tax too high. File it online, or send the paper form with your phone number, signature, date and supporting documents by email, fax or mail.

The process runs through the reason for the abatement, who may apply, the Assessor's action, a possible request for more information, payment of the tax, and an appeal to the Appellate Tax Board. Ask the Assessing Division what timing applies to the appeal step.

State law, M.G.L. c. 59, section 59, sets the filing deadline at the last day to pay the first actual installment without interest. Worcester's actual bills are issued January 1 and due 30 days later, so the window is short and opens near the end of January. Confirm the date with the office every year. Who can apply:

  • The person taxed, or the personal representative of that person's estate.
  • A tenant who pays rent and is bound to pay more than half the taxes.
  • Someone who gets title after January 1, who is treated as a taxpayer for this purpose.
  • A mortgage holder who has paid at least half the tax, during the last 10 days of the abatement period.

Worcester applies the state's statutory exemptions: persons over 70 who meet asset and income limits, surviving spouses with asset limits, blind persons, and owners with service-related disabilities. Qualifying owners must own the property in whole or in part and apply every year.

Applications for many of these can be filed by April 1 or within three months after the bill was sent, whichever is later. Churches, hospitals, schools and cultural groups may qualify under M.G.L. c. 59, section 5, but buying property does not make a religious or charitable group exempt on its own. It has to meet the criteria and file the right forms, which the city posts on its real estate tax page.

The city asks owners of income-producing property to report typical expenses, since the Assessor needs rent data to value those buildings fairly. Separate forms cover apartments, commercial and industrial property, and mixed use.

The information is for the assessor's use and is not public record. Report typical expenses only. If you paid for a big repair such as a new roof, do not report the whole cost in one year. An owner thinking of selling a three-family should expect rent and expense data to matter to the assessment.

sections.h2: Winter and the sale of an older house
sections.html: Worcester winters are hard on roofs, pipes and heating systems, and buyers and inspectors check for that. The city averages about 64 inches of snow a season and is prone to nor'easters. Older buildings raise roof and heating questions, and a cash buyer who takes the house as is can skip repair negotiations. The tax balance still has to be cleared at closing.

Ask the Assessing Division and the Collector's office for a current balance before you list or accept an offer. The city's real estate tax page links to answers on unpaid bills, interest, mortgage company payments and changing the bill to a new owner's name.

Because bills are due 30 days after issue, a mid-year sale usually leaves one bill outstanding. The January 1 owner stays the assessed owner for the fiscal year, so the buyer should receive the seller's bill in care of the new name until the next year.

  • Check which of the four bills for the fiscal year are paid.
  • Ask whether interest has been added to a late bill.
  • Find out if you hold a statutory exemption that the buyer will not get.
  • Ask about the fee and timing for a municipal lien certificate.

Unpaid bills do not stop you from selling. The closing attorney or title company pays what is owed from your proceeds, and you receive the remainder. Gather your bills for the year, note which quarters you have paid, and bring them when you call. Talk to us if you want to sell as is without repairs, and we will go through the numbers with you.

faqs.q: When are Worcester property tax bills due?
faqs.a: Worcester issues bills on July 1, October 1, January 1 and April 1. Payment is due 30 days after each issue date.

faqs.q: What is the Worcester residential tax rate?
faqs.a: Posted rates are $13.28 per $1,000 for residential property and $29.06 per $1,000 for commercial property, with no fiscal year attached. Check your bill for the year and rate.

faqs.q: How do I apply for a Worcester tax abatement?
faqs.a: Use the online application on the city's real estate tax page, or send the paper form to the Assessing Division by email, fax or mail. The deadline follows state law, so confirm it at 508-799-1098.

faqs.q: Why did my Worcester tax bill go up in January?
faqs.a: The July and October bills are preliminary estimates. The January and April bills use your new assessment and rate, so any change from reassessment shows up in those two.

faqs.q: Does Proposition 2 1/2 cap my own tax increase?
faqs.a: No. It limits the total amount the city can raise, plus new construction growth. An individual bill can rise by more than 2.5 percent if your value rose faster than other properties.
